about: Decisions taken for the owner (RULEBOOK rule 27), each with its reason, shown on the review page where he can veto any of them; and at most 7 choices, each phrased as a rule for every page, each with a recommendation already applied in the prototype. Figures in curly braces are filled in by board/build_v3.py from the pages, and an 'assert' is re-checked against the pages on every build (rule 28), so no sentence here can drift from what the pages show.

decisions.title: Who every page is written for
decisions.decision: A man who has tried to cut down or stop and couldn't.
decisions.why: Your notes of 4 and 5 Nov: he already knows he has a problem, and “10 drinks every day” is a different reader from “above the guidelines”. Every number now says which group it counts.

decisions.title: Section order
decisions.decision: Hope number, beliefs, how hard it feels, who gets free and how (who, how they quit, what helps), how quitting goes (life after), the plan, sources. A page with no hope number ({noHero}) opens with its title, then the beliefs, with no line between them. Your own story box shows on the review page only, until you write it.
decisions.why: Your 5 Nov order: one number that creates hope, then beliefs and the graph, then more numbers. The plan comes after the numbers so the reader reaches it having seen that people like him get free. This was a choice last round too; it is one decision now, so you are not asked it twice.

decisions.title: Every “How quitting goes” number you liked is on the pages
decisions.decision: All numbers from the v10 “How quitting goes” section are on the v3 pages, rewritten to the new rules, under “How quitting goes” or “Who gets free, and how”. Where a rule argues against one you liked, it stays even under the recommended off-reader answer, with its Counted label: {likedCards}.
decisions.why: Your 5 Nov note: “more in line with what I want than a bunch of the other stats”. Rule 26 (keep what you liked) wins over the off-reader choice for these; the choice names them in one line.

decisions.title: Every number says who was counted
decisions.decision: A “Counted:” label sits on every number, in plain words, and a short Counted line under each belief proof and plan proof. Number cards about people not checked for addiction come off the pages under the recommended answer to one choice, except the ones you liked in version 10, which stay labelled; kept cards carry an amber label and never appear as a hope, who-gets-free or what-helps number. A belief or plan proof about such people stays, and its Counted line says “not checked for addiction”. A group sorted by questionnaire answers gets its own label: people whose answers showed a likely … problem.
decisions.why: Your 5 Nov note on severity. It also stops a moderation number from coming from people who were never hooked.

decisions.title: One number per line
decisions.decision: Each number gets one sentence of 22 words or fewer with at most two figures; everything else (how many, where, when, what it doesn’t mean) folds under “Based on”.
decisions.why: You couldn’t follow “What helps” on the first read. A cold reader with no context checked every line before you saw it.

decisions.title: What helps, per 100 people
decisions.decision: Every “what helps” number says what happened per 100 people with it and per 100 without it (“27 in 100 vs 12 in 100”), never “×2.3” or “1 in 12” alone. When no study gives a without-it figure, the number sits under How they quit as “What happened with help, no comparison”, marked Weak. Every share of people on a page is written “N in 100”, the hope number too{ownWordsPct}.
decisions.why: You couldn’t follow “What helps” on the first read. Studies of how people read risk numbers find ratios and “1 in N” are the formats readers get wrong most; counts per 100 are read right most often.

decisions.title: Numbers come from one menu
decisions.decision: {nKinds} kinds of number in {nGroups} groups (hope, who gets free, how they quit, what helps, life after). {nPicked} are switched on; every page fills the same kinds, and where a page has no honest number for one, the page says so in one plain line (“Not counted here yet: …”). The {nGeneral} kinds that pool alcohol and other drugs follow the choice about them, not the menu. The Number menu tab shows each page’s number for every kind; switch kinds on or off there, for every page at once.
decisions.why: Your 5 Nov wish to choose from a menu, with general numbers shown once and specific ones per page.

decisions.title: Numbers about every addiction
decisions.decision: Numbers that pool alcohol and other drugs (tries it took, quit with no help, life in the years after) are kept in the Number menu but off the pages, unless you choose otherwise; when shown, they sit under “Alcohol and drugs together”. A page card from the same pooled survey says so on its Counted label and falls under the off-reader choice.
decisions.why: You suggested general numbers shown “somewhere”, and said a one-pager is about one drug. These come from one survey of alcohol and drug problems, so on most pages they would be another drug’s numbers.

decisions.title: How the graph is made, for every addiction
decisions.decision: About {feltRead} posts with a day count read from each addiction’s quit forum (2021–2025, fixed calendar days, 70 per day range); the {feltUsed} that say how the day felt are used. A reader scores how hard that day was, 0 to 10; a second reader, a different AI model, re-scores 15% blind. The headline names the hardest stage (the highest typical day among stages with 25 posts or more) and the stage it is easier from (at least 1.5 points lower, and never back within 1 point after); where no stage qualifies it says “No clear easing”. Version 1 draws a line (a typical day per stage) and a band (where the middle half of scores fell); version 2 draws 20 dots per stage. Under it, “What the body does” draws each body symptom from clinical sources as a bar on one time scale (hour 1 to year 3), darker where it is worst, red for a danger sign.
decisions.why: Your 5 Nov note: true to how people feel, not one study. This is the same recipe on every page, and it says how many posts it rests on and how it is biased.

decisions.title: Phone first, wide on big screens
decisions.decision: Each page is one column on a phone. From 760 px wide, headings move to a left column, numbers sit beside their sentence, and the graph turns from rows into a chart. The review shows both at once.
decisions.why: You said header B fails on a browser and you were unsure how to design for both. Phone first means the narrow screen gets the real design and the wide screen adds to it, so neither is an afterthought.

decisions.title: Beliefs in your two columns, with a test
decisions.decision: 3 to 5 beliefs per page: what you tell yourself, what is also true, and one real-life test for this week. On a wide screen they sit side by side as your columns; on a phone the first two sit side by side as a small table, with the proof and the test under them. Every page links to the Belief test page, where the exercise is explained and done, and entries stay private to each reader.
decisions.why: Your book method and your 5 Nov note: a feature one click away, fully explained.

decisions.title: Danger lines only where a source ties them to the drug
decisions.decision: On the {dangerPages} page: the seizure and DTs rows under the graph (red), one short line in plan step 3 (where the drinking stops), a one-line pointer to “Before you stop” in two card folds (44 in 100, 2–7 days), the same pointer in two belief tests (rows 3 and 4), and the “Before you stop” line above the sources, which names the signs and says: “{emergencyLine}” {noteLine} On the porn page: one line in the erection card’s fold, that a doctor can check for medical causes, with its source. Nowhere else, and never up front.
decisions.why: Your 4 Nov note: only where a source ties the risk to the drug, small, never up front. A safety audit found the plan stops drinking at step 3 while the warning sat in step 5 and at the very bottom, so a heavy daily drinker following the steps would stop before seeing it.

decisions.title: Your five steps, longer
decisions.decision: Your step titles and text stay word for word on every page. Each step now has {planActions} actions for that addiction (it had 2 or 3). In step 1, “the table above” links to the beliefs; in step 5, “me” links to the line under the plan that says who wrote the page.
decisions.why: Your 5 Nov note: the plan should be longer.

decisions.title: Forum posts stay on your machine
decisions.decision: Downloaded posts and scored text stay in ~/.cache. The repo gets counts and scores only, and the build fails if any 8-word run from a post shows up in a public file.
decisions.why: The repo is public, and posts are health disclosures.

decisions.title: Your story box
decisions.decision: The “My experience” placeholder from round 3 stays, but only on the review page, so a reader never sees an empty box.
decisions.why: Cold readers took the placeholder as a sign the page was unfinished. It is yours to write; nothing was removed.

decisions.title: The thought above each number
decisions.decision: Each number has one line above it: the thought it answers, written by us, 14 words or fewer, in the second person.
decisions.why: It helps a reader find the number that is about him. Last round this was a choice; rules 8 and 16 already require the line, so asking it again was the same detail twice.

decisions.title: A page with no hope number
decisions.decision: Where no study counts people hooked on it who got free ({noHero}), the page has no big number: its title, then the beliefs. “Who gets free, and how” says plainly what no study has counted yet.
decisions.why: Rule 15 asks for a number that creates hope; the nearest porn figures are a statistical grouping and students, and a gap as the first words is no hope either.

decisions.title: Who “me” is
decisions.decision: Under the plan: “Written by the coach who runs this site.” Your step 5 says “1-on-1 help from me”, and cold readers asked who that is.
decisions.why: A placeholder until the brand name is set (docs/product/brand.md); change the words in a note and every page follows.

decisions.title: Sources numbered as the page cites them
decisions.decision: Each page’s source list runs 1, 2, 3 … in the order the page first cites them, with no gaps; the forum posts behind the graph are one entry.
decisions.why: Cold readers asked what was cut when the list skipped a number, and saw the forum listed twice.

choices.rule: The big hope number on every page is:
choices.why: Both numbers stay on every page, together, in one view; this picks which one comes first and leads the dot grid. Your own rule 15 says lead with one number that creates hope, so I recommend the lifetime projection ({heroProj}), with the head count right under it ({heroCount}). Rule 10 (cautious estimate first) came from reviewers, not from you; with the head count big, nicotine would open on 19 in 100. This is a judgment call: the projection is a model that likely runs high, and the page says so once, on the chip under it. Pages with no hope number ({noHero}) open at the beliefs either way.

options.label: The lifetime projection, the count under it
The head count, the projection under it

choices.rule: Numbers that mix every drug together (tries it took, used no help, life in the years after):
choices.why: One US survey of people who beat a drink or drug problem also reports numbers for everyone together, not split by drug. The pages show its alcohol-only and weed-only numbers. I recommend leaving the mixed ones off. {mixedLine}

options.label: Show on the pages the survey covers

choices.rule: Where an app publishes day-by-day check-in data (for now only {appPages}: I Am Sober), show it under the forum graph:
choices.why: I recommend leaving it out: it counts heavy drinkers quitting or cutting back, not checked for addiction, and cutting back is the angle you called dangerous on 5 Nov. Its peak is also the quit day, not days 2–3 as in the posts.

choices.rule: Number cards about people who are not the reader: not checked as hooked (students, ordinary smokers), people never or still hooked mixed in, or cutting down instead of quitting:
choices.why: Your rule: every page is for a man who is hooked. So I recommend taking all {offCards} off every page; the list below names each card and its reason. This choice covers number cards only: a belief proof or plan proof about such people stays, with a Counted line that says “not checked for addiction”.

choices.rule: Which version of each section every page uses:
choices.why: Version 1 is your 2025 sheet with the rules applied; version 2 counts people (dots, a fact box). My picks, shown under “Your picks”: the hope number from version 2 (the dot grid shows what is counted and what is projected), the graph from version 1 (a line for the typical day; it names the hardest stage and when it gets easier, or says there is no clear easing), everything else from version 1. Change any section with the blue bar above it.

graph.title: The recipe, the same for every addiction
text: Posts from that addiction's quit forum, downloaded from the Arctic Shift public archive (reddit.com blocks this machine): every post from fixed calendar days, 2021 to 2025, so no season or weekday is favoured.
Only posts that give a day count (“Day 12”, “3 weeks”, or the forum's day badge). 70 posts drawn at random for each of 15 day bins, from day 1 to year 2 and on: about 1,050 per addiction.

An AI reader scored each post: how hard the writer says staying off is today, 0 (no struggle) to 10 (can barely hold on), and which symptoms they name. Posts about a slip, or that say nothing about how today feels, are left out.

15% of posts were scored again by a second reader that never saw the first scores, once by the same model and once by a different one (Claude Sonnet). The table below gives how often they landed within 1 point.
Body symptoms under the graph come from clinical sources, drawn as ranges, never as one curve. A lab test of how strongly cues pull is never drawn as craving.

graph.title: What it can't tell you
text: People who post are not everyone who quits. People who find it easy have less reason to post, and people post more on hard days, so the curve likely runs higher than for quitters in general.
Later days are mostly milestone posts. People who slipped earlier are no longer in them.
The readers are AI models, not the writers rating themselves. Two models agreeing shows the scores are consistent, not that they are what the writers would have said.

graph.title: Your “1,000 people a day”: a proposal for the app
text: One question a day after the quit date, “How hard was today?”, on the same 0 to 10 scale, plus optional symptom taps. Each reader sees his own line over the page's curve.

Opt-in, counted without names, and shown per day bin only once 30 people have reached it; until then the page keeps the forum curve. Nothing is built: the full proposal is in 08-v3/daily-log-proposal.md.

kept: The template page (version 10, https://claude.ai/artifact/8D5nSxoACGvVn7PBRHbCus) and the first board (https://claude.ai/artifact/9wfvJfSHm3BNTUXmijH7GK) are untouched, with all your marks.
Their files are untouched: 06-template.json, 07-mirror-stats/*.json, community/leaves-stages.json, board/build.py, build_template.py, template.html, template-v2.html.
Nothing was removed from the old pages. Old numbers, beliefs and round-2 milestones this prototype does not show are on the “Not on this page” tab, grouped, each with its reason.
Betting, phone, sugar and cocaine are not in this prototype; their pages stay as they are on the template page.
The app is untouched: nothing was built in it (a possible rebuild of the app is still undecided).

weak.title: The porn page is a draft: its science is the thinnest
weak.text: No study counts men hooked on porn who got free, projects it over a lifetime, gives the age it ended, or counts who quit without help. So the page has no hope number: it opens at the beliefs, and “Who gets free, and how” says plainly what is not counted. Its other numbers are small (one forum’s journals, one church-based trial of 26 men). Under the recommended off-reader answer these porn cards come off: {offPorn}; these stay because you liked them in version 10: {likedPorn}.

weak.title: The lifetime “get free” numbers are projections, and they lead
weak.text: {heroProj} are a model built from ages people remembered. The authors say people over-report getting free and the survey missed people in prisons and hospitals, so the real shares are likely lower. They lead the page because your rule 15 asks for hope first; the head count sits right under each, and the projection carries one chip, said once: worked out, not counted, likely runs high.

weak.title: The felt-difficulty graph is posts, not people
weak.text: It rests on {feltUsed} usable posts per addiction, scored by AI readers, not the writers. People who post are not everyone who quits and likely struggle more. A stage under 25 posts is drawn hollow, with its post count, and not used to call the hardest stretch ({fewStages}).

weak.title: Two AI readers agreeing is not the same as being right
weak.text: A second, different model landed within 1 point of the first {agreeCross} of the time. That shows the scores are consistent. Nobody checked them against what the writers would have said.

weak.title: The I Am Sober app curve counts heavy drinkers who kept using the app
weak.text: Members who drank 21 to 70 a week, not checked for addiction, quitting or cutting back. {app1} wrote a check-in on day 1 and {app30} on day 30, so later days describe the ones still going. Off the page under the recommended answer.

weak.title: Most “who gets free” numbers are surveys of memory
weak.text: Ages and tries are what people remembered years later, in US surveys. None is a trial.

weak.title: The “also true” lines and the tests are written by Claude
weak.text: They follow your method and every proof under them is sourced, but no reader has tried them yet. The cold readers here were AI models reading screenshots, not real readers.

weak.title: Not in this prototype: betting, phone, sugar, cocaine
weak.text: Their open doubts stand as before (betting 92% rests on 25 men; sugar's top numbers are about weight loss; phone numbers count ordinary users). They stay on the template page until the template is locked.

byline: Written by the coach who runs this site.
